title: 22. Interview: Design Google Drive
summary: Interview Q&A for Design Google Drive — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Design Google Drive interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Trade-offs Discussed
sections.body:
- **Block-level vs file-level dedup**: 4 MB blocks catch more matches (one changed block doesn't waste the whole file) but cost more metadata (one hash per 4 MB vs one per file). At Google's scale, block-level saves ~30 % vs file-level's ~10 %.
- **Spanner vs Cassandra for metadata**: ACID + global consistency (Spanner) vs eventual consistency + higher throughput (Cassandra). File metadata needs ACID — a half-committed rename is a bug. Spanner's trade-off is higher cost.
- **Push (full payload) vs pull-on-push (notification + delta)**: push is simpler but wastes bandwidth; pull-on-push scales better and supports batched deltas.
- **Last-writer-wins vs OT vs CRDTs for conflicts**: LWW is simplest but loses work for binary files; OT/CRDTs preserve edits but only work for text. Hybrid: LWW for binaries, OT for Docs.
- **Resumable upload via Content-Range vs multipart/form-data**: Content-Range supports partial retry and parallel chunk upload; multipart is simpler but all-or-nothing.

sections.title: Q1. Why does Google Drive use 4 MB blocks instead of file-level dedup?
sections.body:
**Answer:** File-level dedup only catches identical whole files — two users uploading the same Windows ISO. But many real cases involve files that share most blocks but differ slightly: a PowerPoint template filled in by 1 000 different users (each slide deck is 99 % identical template, 1 % unique content), an OS image with one config changed, a large video re-encoded with one extra second. With 4 MB block-level dedup, only the changed 4 MB blocks are stored once; the common blocks are deduped across all users. Google's actual reported savings is ~30 % of total bytes (vs ~10 % for file-level). Trade-off: 4 MB blocks cost 32 bytes of hash metadata per block (0.0008 % overhead), and the Block Index grows large (100 EB / 4 MB × 32 bytes = 800 TB index), but that's a small cost vs the 30 EB storage saved. The block size is also tuned for upload throughput — 4 MB is large enough to amortize per-request overhead (TLS handshake, hash computation) but small enough for fine-grained dedup and resumable uploads.
**Visual:**
```
File-level dedup:    two slightly different PDFs -> stored twice (no savings)
                     [PDF1 100MB][PDF2 100MB]                = 200MB

Block-level dedup:   two slightly different PDFs share 24 of 25 blocks
                     [B1][B2]...[B24][B25']      (only B25' new)
                     total stored = 100MB + 4MB  = 104MB      (48% savings)
```

sections.title: Q2. How does the resumable upload protocol handle network drops mid-upload of a 5 TB file?
sections.body:
**Answer:** A 5 TB upload at 100 MB/s takes ~14 hours — network interruptions are guaranteed. The protocol: (1) Client calls `POST /uploads/init` to get an `upload_id` (valid for 7 days). (2) Client splits the file into 4 MB blocks, computes SHA-256 of each. (3) Client calls `/check-blocks` with the hashes — server returns which are already stored (from prior partial uploads or dedup). (4) Client uploads missing blocks one by one via `PUT /uploads/{upload_id}/blocks/{hash}` with `Content-Range: bytes 0-4194303/*`. Each PUT is idempotent (same hash → same result). (5) If the connection drops at block 47/256, the client retries only block 47 — server tracks per-upload_id which blocks are stored. (6) For parallelism, the client uploads multiple blocks concurrently across separate TCP connections (HTTP/2 multiplexing helps). (7) After all blocks are uploaded, the client calls `POST /files` with the hash list to create the metadata entry. (8) If the client crashes and restarts, it can resume by calling `/check-blocks` — server reports which blocks are missing, client uploads only those. This is essentially the design of Google Drive's actual upload protocol (and S3 multipart upload, Azure Block Blob).
**Visual:**
```
Client                                Server
  | --- POST /uploads/init ----------> |
  | <------- {upload_id: "u123"} ---- |
  | --- POST /check-blocks hashes --->|
  | <------- {missing: [b47, b48]} -- |
  | --- PUT /blocks/b47 (Content-Range 0-4MB/*) -->|
  | --- PUT /blocks/b48 ------------->|  (parallel)
  | <----- 200 OK -----              |
  | <----- 200 OK -------------------|
  | === connection drops at b49 ===   |
  | (retry only b49)                  |
  | --- PUT /blocks/b49 ------------->|
  | <----- 200 OK -------------------|
  | --- POST /files (hash list) ----->|
  | <------- {file_id: "f42"} -------|
```

sections.title: Q3. How does conflict resolution work when two devices edit the same file offline?
sections.body:
**Answer:** Each device tracks the `base_version` it last saw from the server. On commit, the client sends `base_version = N`. The server compares: (1) If `base_version == current_version`, fast-path commit — no conflict, increment version, append to event log. (2) If `base_version < current_version`, another device committed first — conflict. For **binary files** (images, PDFs, Office docs), the server uses **last-writer-wins**: the new commit becomes the latest version, the previous latest is preserved as a prior version (so the user can manually merge later). The `conflict=true` flag tells the client to show a "Conflict resolved — both versions kept" notification. For **Google Docs** (text), the server uses **operational transform (OT)**: each edit is a series of operations (insert char at pos N, delete range), and the server transforms the incoming operations against the operations that have already been applied. This preserves both users' edits non-destructively — both "Alice added 'hello' at position 5" and "Bob added 'world' at position 11" are applied. For **folders** (rename/move conflicts), the server detects if two devices renamed the same file to different names and prompts the user. CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) are an alternative to OT for collaborative text — used by Notion, Linear, and others — but Google Docs still uses OT for historical reasons.
**Visual:**
```
Device A (laptop): edits offline from v3 -> commits v4
Device B (phone):  edits offline from v3 -> commits v4 (CONFLICT)

Server:
  v3: original
  v4: laptop's version  <-- current
  v5: phone's version   <-- LWW, conflict=true, both kept in history

Client UI: "Conflict on doc.pdf — we kept both versions. Compare?"
```

sections.title: Q4. How would you design the sync notification protocol to handle 1 B users with 3 devices each?
sections.body:
**Answer:** Pure server-push of full file payloads is infeasible (3 B devices × per-change payload = exabytes/day). The design is **pull-on-push**: (1) Each device maintains a long-lived connection to a Notification Service (WebSocket for web/desktop, FCM for Android, APNs for iOS). (2) When a file changes, the Sync Service appends to the user's event log and sends a tiny "wake up, LSN=42" notification (a few bytes) to all of the user's other devices via FCM/APNs/WebSocket. (3) Each device, on receiving the notification, calls `GET /sync/changes?since_lsn={last_seen}` to pull the actual delta (file IDs + new versions, not full file content). (4) The device then downloads the changed blocks as needed. This scales because: notifications are tiny (3 B devices × 10 changes/day × 32 bytes = 1 GB/day of notification traffic), and the actual data transfer is on-demand (only when the user opens the app or the file). For devices without push capability (old desktop clients), fall back to long-polling every 30 s. Connection servers are sharded by `user_id` (like WhatsApp's Erlang connection layer) — a single connection server handles ~1 M concurrent WebSocket connections. Total: ~3 000 connection servers globally. Redis pub/sub fans out per-user notifications to the right connection server.
**Visual:**
```
File change event:
  Sync Service -> append user event_log LSN=42
              -> Redis PUBLISH user:alice:notify {lsn: 42}
                                      |
              +-----------------------+----------------+
              v                       v                v
       Conn Server 1            Conn Server 2    FCM/APNs Gateway
       (WebSocket to laptop)    (WebSocket to    (push to phone)
                                desktop2)
              |                       |                |
              v                       v                v
       Laptop wakes,           Desktop2 wakes,   Phone wakes,
       GET /sync/changes       GET /sync/        GET /sync/
       ?since_lsn=41           changes?since=    changes?since=
                              41                41
              |
              v
       Pulls delta: {file-1 v4}
       Downloads changed blocks
```

sections.title: Q5. How does block-level dedup affect privacy — could one user learn that another user has the…
sections.body:
**Answer:** This is a real concern: a "confirmation of existence" attack. If an attacker can check whether a specific hash exists in the Block Index, they can confirm whether a target user has a particular file (e.g., a known sensitive document). Mitigations: (1) **Hash check requires auth**: `POST /check-blocks` requires a valid user OAuth token; the server only returns missing hashes that the caller has upload rights to. But this alone isn't enough — an attacker with their own account can still probe. (2) **Threshold dedup**: only return "already exists" if `ref_count > N` (e.g., > 5) — common files (OS ISOs, public documents) get deduped, but unique files don't reveal anything. Trade-off: this loses some dedup savings for files shared by 2–5 users. (3) **Convergent encryption**: the client encrypts each block with a key derived from the block's hash (so identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext across users). The server can dedup without ever seeing plaintext. But the server still sees the ciphertext hash, which is the same as the plaintext hash for dedup purposes — so this doesn't fully solve the confirmation attack. (4) **Proof-of-ownership**: before reporting "block exists", require the client to upload a small proof that they actually have the block (e.g., a Merkle proof of a specific byte range). This prevents blind hash probing. (5) **Rate limit hash checks**: max 100 checks per user per minute, anomaly detection on suspicious patterns. Google Drive and Dropbox use a combination of these; the exact defense is not publicly documented.
**Visual:**
```
Naive (insecure):
  Attacker: POST /check-blocks ["sha256:abc..."] -> {missing: []}
  Attacker: "Alice has the file with hash abc... (confirmed)"

Defended:
  Attacker: POST /check-blocks ["sha256:abc..."]
  Server: ref_count=1 (unique file) -> respond "missing" even if exists
  OR: require proof-of-ownership (Merkle proof of byte range)
  OR: rate-limit + anomaly detection
```

sections.title: Q6. How does Google Drive enforce quota atomically with file commits?
sections.body:
**Answer:** A user could otherwise race: upload a 5 GB file when they have 1 GB free, by submitting two commits in parallel — each check sees "1 GB free" and both succeed, putting the user over quota. The fix is a Spanner transaction wrapping: (1) `SELECT bytes_used, bytes_limit FROM user_quota WHERE user_id = ?` (with a row-level lock), (2) check `bytes_used + new_file_size <= bytes_limit`, (3) if yes, `INSERT INTO files ...` and `UPDATE user_quota SET bytes_used = bytes_used + new_file_size`, (4) commit transaction. Spanner's external consistency (via TrueTime + Paxos) guarantees the lock is held atomically — no two parallel commits can both pass the check. For deletions, the reverse: `UPDATE user_quota SET bytes_used = bytes_used - file_size` in the same transaction as `UPDATE files SET deleted_at = now()`. The trade-off is throughput: a single user's commits are serialized through the quota row, but that's fine — one user's commit rate is naturally low. For batch uploads, the client can pre-reserve quota (e.g., reserve 5 GB for an upload_id, then commit incrementally) to amortize the per-file transaction cost. Google Drive's actual implementation is more sophisticated — quotas are checked at block upload time too, so a user can't upload 5 GB of blocks then fail the metadata commit (which would orphan the blocks).
**Visual:**
```
Without transaction (vulnerable):
  T1: SELECT bytes_used (1GB free)   |   T2: SELECT bytes_used (1GB free)
  T1: INSERT file (5GB)              |   T2: INSERT file (5GB)
  T1: UPDATE bytes_used += 5GB       |   T2: UPDATE bytes_used += 5GB
  => bytes_used = 11GB (over quota!) but both commits succeeded

With Spanner transaction:
  T1: BEGIN -> SELECT FOR UPDATE -> (locked) -> check -> INSERT -> UPDATE -> COMMIT
                                                       |
  T2: BEGIN -> SELECT FOR UPDATE -> (BLOCKED until T1 commits)
                                                       |
  T2: resumes -> sees bytes_used=6GB -> check fails -> ABORT
```

sections.title: Q7. How would you handle a "shared with me" view that scales to millions of files shared with…
sections.body:
**Answer:** A naive `SELECT * FROM acl_entries WHERE principal = 'user:alice'` would return millions of rows and be slow. Design: (1) **Denormalize** at ACL-grant time: when a file is shared with Alice, also insert a row into `shared_with_me (user_id, file_id, shared_at, shared_by)`. This duplicate table is the source of truth for the "Shared with me" view. (2) **Index** by `(user_id, shared_at DESC)` so the view (sorted by share date) is a fast index range scan. (3) **Pagination** via cursor: `WHERE user_id = ? AND shared_at < ? ORDER BY shared_at DESC LIMIT 50`. (4) **Cache** the first page in Redis (`shared_first_page:{user_id}`, TTL 60 s) — most users only view the first page. (5) **Materialized view** for filters: if the user filters by file type, maintain `shared_with_me_by_type (user_id, mime_type, file_id, shared_at)`. (6) **Async reindexing** for renames: if a shared file is renamed by its owner, the `shared_with_me` row's `name` field becomes stale — we either re-index via a Kafka event or always join to `files` at read time (one extra lookup). (7) **Trash propagation**: if a shared file is trashed by the owner, all `shared_with_me` entries get `deleted_at = now()` via a single bulk update + Kafka event. Google Drive's actual implementation uses a similar denormalization pattern, and the "Shared with me" view has sub-second load time even for power users with millions of shared files.
**Visual:**
```
acl_entries (normalized, slow for "shared with me"):
  (file_id, principal)   <- millions of rows for popular user
  SELECT * WHERE principal = 'user:alice'  -> slow scan

shared_with_me (denormalized, fast):
  (user_id, file_id, shared_at, shared_by, name)  indexed by (user_id, shared_at DESC)
  SELECT * WHERE user_id = alice ORDER BY shared_at DESC LIMIT 50  -> index range scan, <50ms

Cache:
  Redis: shared_first_page:alice -> [file_id_1, ..., file_id_50] TTL 60s
```

sections.title: Q1. A user uploads a 100 GB file and the connection drops at 60 GB. They restart their laptop.…
sections.body:
**Answer:** Two layers of resumability: (1) **Per-block idempotency**: each 4 MB block was uploaded via `PUT /uploads/{upload_id}/blocks/{hash}` — the server tracks which blocks are stored per `upload_id` (valid for 7 days). When the client restarts, it calls `POST /uploads/{upload_id}/check-blocks` with all 25 600 block hashes; the server responds with the ~10 000 missing hashes (blocks 15 000-25 600, roughly). The client uploads only those, not the first 60 GB. (2) **Client-side state**: the client persists the `upload_id` and the list of block hashes to local disk (in a `.drive_upload_meta` file or in the client's SQLite cache). Without this, the client would have to re-hash the whole 100 GB file on restart — feasible but slow. With it, the client can resume in seconds. (3) **Failure during a single block PUT**: if the connection drops mid-block (e.g., 2 MB of a 4 MB block uploaded), the client retries the whole block PUT with `Content-Range: bytes 0-4194303/*` — the server detects the existing partial upload and overwrites it. (4) **Final commit**: after all blocks are confirmed, the client calls `POST /files` with the full hash list. If the laptop crashes before this call, the blocks are orphaned (server reclaims them after 7 days via a janitor job that GCs `upload_id`s with no file commit). The user experience: "Upload paused — will resume when you restart" → on restart, upload continues from 60 GB, not 0.
**Visual:**
```
Laptop restart, 60GB of 100GB uploaded:
  Client reads .drive_upload_meta -> upload_id="u123", 25600 block hashes
  Client: POST /uploads/u123/check-blocks [all 25600 hashes]
  Server: {missing: [hash_15000, hash_15001, ..., hash_25599]}  (10k missing)
  Client: resumes upload at block 15000
  ...
  Client: POST /files {hashes: [...]} -> {file_id: "f42"}
```

sections.title: Q2. A user shares a folder with 100 sub-folders and 10 000 files with another user. How do you…
sections.body:
**Answer:** Naive approach: 10 001 inserts into `acl_entries` (one per file/folder). For 10 000 simultaneous shares this is slow (1-2 s) and produces 10 000 sync events. Better: (1) **ACL inheritance**: store ACLs only at the folder level — `acl_entries (folder_id, principal, role)`. At access time, walk up the parent chain until root, checking ACLs at each level. If any ancestor grants the principal the required role, access is granted. This is how POSIX filesystems and Google Drive actually work. (2) **Single insert**: sharing a folder = one insert into `acl_entries (folder_id, principal, role)`. (3) **Sync event**: one event "acl_changed folder_id=X" with the principal. The recipient's client fetches the folder tree on demand (lazy expansion), not all 10 000 files at once. (4) **Cache invalidation**: the Permission Service caches `can(user, file, action)` results in Redis. On ACL change, invalidate `acl:*:{folder_id}` and all descendants — implemented by maintaining `acl_children:{folder_id}` set (refresh every 5 min) and pipeline DEL. (5) **Notification**: one notification "Folder 'Project X' was shared with you" rather than 10 000 "File Y was shared" notifications. (6) **Quota / storage**: ACL inheritance has zero storage cost vs storing one row per file (10 000 rows saved). Trade-off: the permission check walks up the tree (avg depth ~5) — 5 lookups per access. Cache hits make this ~1 lookup in practice.
**Visual:**
```
Naive (10,000 inserts):
  INSERT acl (folder, alice, editor)
  INSERT acl (file1, alice, editor)
  INSERT acl (file2, alice, editor)
  ... 10,000 rows

Inherited (1 insert):
  INSERT acl (folder, alice, editor)
  
  Permission check for file42 (depth 3):
    can(alice, file42, read)?
    -> check acl(file42, alice)        MISS
    -> check acl(parent_folder, alice) MISS
    -> check acl(grandparent, alice)   HIT (editor -> can read)
    -> return true   (3 lookups, all cached in Redis after first hit)
```

sections.title: Q3. A user has 1 million files in their Drive. How do you keep the client's folder view fast?
sections.body:
**Answer:** A naive "load all files on app open" would download 1 GB of metadata and take 30+ seconds. Design: (1) **Lazy folder expansion**: the client only fetches the immediate children of the folder the user is viewing, via `GET /folders/{id}/children?cursor=...&limit=100`. Browsing deeper fetches more. (2) **Local SQLite cache**: the client maintains a local copy of the file tree (filenames, parents, modified_at) synced via the event log. Folder opens read from SQLite (instant); the event log keeps it up-to-date. (3) **Incremental sync on app open**: client calls `GET /sync/changes?since_lsn={last_seen}` — if 100 files changed in the last hour, only 100 events are downloaded, not 1 M. The client updates its SQLite cache. (4) **Pagination**: large folders return 100 files per page; infinite scroll fetches more. (5) **Search as the primary navigation**: for power users, search (Elasticsearch over filenames + content) is faster than drilling through folders. Google Drive's actual UI emphasizes search over folder browsing for this reason. (6) **Background prefetch**: when the user is in folder A, prefetch folder A's children's children (one level deep) in the background, so navigating deeper feels instant. (7) **Thumbnail lazy-loading**: only fetch thumbnails for files in the viewport (intersection observer). With this design, the app opens in <1 s even with 1 M files, and folder navigation is sub-100 ms.
**Visual:**
```
App open:
  Client: GET /sync/changes?since_lsn=12345
  Server: {changes: [100 events], latest_lsn: 12445}
  Client: updates local SQLite cache (1 ms per event)
  Client: shows "My Drive" with first 100 children from SQLite (instant)

User clicks into folder "Projects":
  Client: SELECT * FROM files WHERE parent='Projects' LIMIT 100  (SQLite, <5ms)
  Client: fetches thumbnails for visible files (lazy)
  Client: background-prefetches "Projects/Sub1" children (1 HTTP call)
```

sections.title: Q4. The CEO wants end-to-end encryption (E2EE) — server can't see file contents. How does that…
sections.body:
**Answer:** E2EE fundamentally changes several subsystems: (1) **Client-side encryption**: each file is encrypted with a symmetric key (AES-256-GCM) on the client before upload. The server stores only ciphertext blocks. (2) **Key management**: each file gets a unique data encryption key (DEK), which is itself encrypted with the user's master key (KEK) derived from their password (PBKDF2/scrypt). The encrypted DEK is stored in metadata. The server never sees the KEK or DEK. (3) **Deduplication breaks**: with E2EE, two users with the same plaintext file produce different ciphertext (different keys), so block-level dedup is impossible. Convergent encryption (key = hash of plaintext) restores dedup but enables confirmation-of-existence attacks (see Q5). Trade-off: lose ~30 % storage savings. (4) **Search breaks**: server can't index ciphertext. Client-side search requires downloading the file index (encrypted) — feasible for filenames, harder for full-text content (would require client-side search index, ~10 % of file size). (5) **Sharing**: to share a file with Bob, Alice encrypts the DEK with Bob's public key and stores it in metadata. Bob's client decrypts the DEK with his private key, then decrypts the file. This requires a PKI for user public keys. (6) **Thumbnails**: server can't generate thumbnails of ciphertext — client generates and uploads an encrypted thumbnail. (7) **Collaborative editing (Google Docs)**: OT/CRDTs work on encrypted operations if the server never needs to interpret them, but this is complex (the server can't merge conflicting operations without seeing them). E2EE is fundamentally incompatible with server-side OT — Google Docs would have to fall back to LWW. Services like Tresorit, Proton Drive, and Mega implement E2EE; Google Drive does not (it uses transport + at-rest encryption but the server can read contents for search, malware scanning, ML features).
**Visual:**
```
Without E2EE:                          With E2EE:
  Client uploads plaintext block       Client encrypts block with DEK (AES-256-GCM)
  Server stores, dedups, indexes       Server stores ciphertext only (no dedup)
  Server can search content            Search: client downloads encrypted index
  Server generates thumbnails          Thumbnails: client generates + uploads encrypted
  Sharing: server reads + re-sends     Sharing: client re-encrypts DEK with Bob's pubkey

Trade-offs:
  + Privacy: server breach doesn't expose content
  - No dedup (-30% storage efficiency)
  - No server-side search, thumbnails, malware scan
  - More complex sharing (PKI required)
  - No collaborative editing (OT breaks)
```

sections.title: Q5. A user is on a slow 3G connection (100 KB/s) and wants to download a 1 GB file. How do you…
sections.body:
**Answer:** Downloading 1 GB at 100 KB/s takes ~3 hours — too slow, and any interruption restarts from scratch. Optimizations: (1) **Resumable download with Range requests**: client sends `GET /files/{id}/data` with `Range: bytes=0-4194303` for the first 4 MB block; on interruption, resumes from the last received byte. The server supports `Accept-Ranges: bytes`. (2) **Parallel chunked download**: open 4 parallel connections, each downloading a different 25 % of the file. This 4× the effective throughput (if the bottleneck is per-connection, not total bandwidth). HTTP/2 multiplexing helps here. (3) **Adaptive block size**: on a stable fast connection, use 16 MB blocks (less per-request overhead); on a flaky 3G connection, drop to 1 MB blocks (less to re-download on interruption). The client measures RTT + loss rate and adjusts. (4) **Compression**: if the file is compressible (text, Office docs), the server compresses on-the-fly with gzip or Brotli — 50-70 % size reduction. Already-compressed formats (JPEG, MP4) skip this. (5) **Prioritized partial download**: for PDFs and videos, fetch the first few pages/seconds first so the user can start viewing while the rest downloads. (6) **Background download with progress UI**: show "Downloading 1 of 256 blocks..." with ETA and a pause/resume button. (7) **CDN edge caching**: if the file is popular (shared link), the CDN serves it from a POP closer to the user, reducing RTT from 200 ms to 20 ms. Combined, these can reduce effective download time from 3 hours to ~30 minutes on 3G, with full resumability.
**Visual:**
```
Naive: 1 request, 1GB, 3 hours, no resume
  Client ---GET /file/data (1GB)---> Server
  (3G drops at 600MB) -> restart from 0

Optimized: 4 parallel resumable chunked downloads
  Client --Range: 0-256MB----> Server (parallel conn 1)
  Client --Range: 256-512MB--> Server (parallel conn 2)
  Client --Range: 512-768MB--> Server (parallel conn 3)
  Client --Range: 768-1024MB-> Server (parallel conn 4)
  (3G drops at 150MB on conn 1) -> resume Range: 150-256MB only
  Adaptive: drop block size from 16MB to 1MB on flaky signal
  Total: ~30 min, fully resumable
```

sections.title: Q6. Your Block Index database (Spanner) is hitting its write throughput limit during a global…
sections.body:
**Answer:** Spanner's per-table write throughput is bounded by the size of the largest tablet (~4 GB → ~few thousand writes/s per tablet). With 100 EB of blocks and a 32-byte index entry per block, the Block Index table is ~800 TB — auto-split into ~200 000 tablets, theoretically supporting millions of writes/s. But hot hashes (popular files uploaded simultaneously) concentrate writes on one tablet. Mitigations: (1) **Migrate Block Index to Bigtable**: Bigtable is optimized for high-throughput KV writes (millions/s per cluster) with auto-sharding by row key. Spanner's strength (ACID transactions) is wasted on the Block Index, which only needs atomic increments. Bigtable is the better tool. (2) **Cache hot hashes in Redis**: a small Redis cluster (100 GB, ~10 M entries) caches positive lookups (hash exists), absorbing 90 % of read traffic. Writes still go to Bigtable. (3) **Batch ref_count updates**: instead of incrementing `ref_count` on every block PUT, batch updates in memory and flush every 1 s (eventual consistency for ref_count is fine — it's only used for GC). (4) **Shard by hash prefix**: if a single hash becomes truly hot (e.g., Windows ISO uploaded by 1000 users in 1 min), shard the ref_count across `ref_count_0`, `ref_count_1`, ..., `ref_count_15` (16 sub-counters), and sum at read time. This 16× the write throughput for that one row. (5) **Pre-allocate known-popular blocks**: for OS ISOs and other known-shared files, pre-load their hashes into the Block Index before peak. (6) **Rate-limit the API**: if all else fails, throttle uploads per user (10 MB/s) during the spike to protect the Block Index. The right answer is usually (1) + (2): use Bigtable for the Block Index, Redis for hot reads, accept eventual consistency on ref_count.
**Visual:**
```
Before (Spanner Block Index):
  1 hot hash "windows.iso_block42" -> all writes hit one tablet
  Tablet overloaded: 5k writes/s limit hit, 503s returned

After (Bigtable + Redis + sharded counters):
  Block Index in Bigtable: auto-sharded by row key, millions of writes/s
  Redis cache: 90% of reads hit cache (hot hashes)
  Sharded counters: ref_count_0..15 for one hot hash, 16x throughput
  Batch flush: ref_count updates buffered 1s, flushed in batch
```

sections.title: Q7. A user reports their file "disappeared" — it's not in their Drive, not in Trash. How do you…
sections.body:
**Answer:** This is a "ghost file" incident — the metadata and the user's view are inconsistent. Debug steps: (1) **Check Trash and Trash expirations**: is the file in Trash with `deleted_at` within 30 days? `SELECT * FROM files WHERE owner_id = ? AND deleted_at IS NOT NULL ORDER BY deleted_at DESC LIMIT 100`. If found, restore. (2) **Check ownership transfer**: was the file transferred to another account? `SELECT * FROM file_ownership_history WHERE file_id = ?`. (3) **Check ACL revocation**: was the file shared with the user, then the owner unshared? `SELECT * FROM acl_history WHERE file_id = ? AND principal = 'user:{alice}'`. The user saw it in "Shared with me" yesterday, but the owner revoked access. (4) **Check the event log**: `SELECT * FROM user_event_log WHERE user_id = ? AND file_id = ? ORDER BY lsn`. This shows every event (created, modified, deleted, unshared) for that file from the user's perspective. If there's a `file_deleted` event the user doesn't remember, that's the smoking gun. (5) **Check parent folder**: was the parent folder moved to Trash? Files inherit Trash state from parents. `SELECT deleted_at FROM files WHERE file_id = (SELECT parent_folder_id FROM files WHERE file_id = ?)`. (6) **Check client-side state**: the user's local SQLite cache might be stale — ask them to refresh / re-sync. (7) **Check for orphaned blocks**: if the file metadata was deleted but blocks remain, a janitor job can reconstruct the file from `block_index` entries with `ref_count > 0` but no file reference. (8) **Recovery**: if the file's metadata exists with `deleted_at != null` and within 30 days, restore via `UPDATE files SET deleted_at = null WHERE file_id = ?`. If outside 30 days, the metadata is hard-deleted but blocks may still be in Colossus (Colossus has its own retention) — manual recovery via support ticket. Google Drive's actual support flow includes a "file recovery" tool that searches 90 days of metadata history.
**Visual:**
```
Debug flow:
  1. SELECT * FROM files WHERE owner=alice AND deleted_at IS NOT NULL -> in Trash?
       YES -> restore, done.
       NO  -> continue
  2. SELECT * FROM acl_history WHERE file_id=X AND principal='user:alice'
       -> unshared 2 hours ago? -> "Owner revoked access" -> tell user
  3. SELECT * FROM user_event_log WHERE user_id=alice AND file_id=X
       -> file_deleted event by alice at 3am? -> "You deleted it" -> check Trash
  4. SELECT deleted_at FROM files WHERE file_id=parent(X)
       -> parent folder was trashed at 3am? -> "Parent folder in Trash"
  5. None of above -> escalate to engineering, check block_index for orphaned blocks
```

quiz.question: Why does Google Drive use 4 MB blocks instead of file-level dedup?
options: Pure server-push of full file payloads is infeasible (3 B devices × per-change payload = exabytes/day).
This is a "ghost file" incident — the metadata and the user's view are inconsistent.
Downloading 1 GB at 100 KB/s takes ~3 hours — too slow, and any interruption restarts from scratch.
File-level dedup only catches identical whole files — two users uploading the same Windows ISO.
quiz.explanation: File-level dedup only catches identical whole files — two users uploading the same Windows ISO. But many real cases involve files that share most blocks but differ slightly: a PowerPoint template filled in by 1 000 different users (each slide deck is 99 % identical template, 1 % unique content), an OS image with one config changed, a large video re-encoded with one extra second.

quiz.explanation: A 5 TB upload at 100 MB/s takes ~14 hours — network interruptions are guaranteed. The protocol: (1) Client calls POST /uploads/init to get an upload_id (valid for 7 days). (2) Client splits the file into 4 MB blocks, computes SHA-256 of each.

quiz.explanation: This is a real concern: a "confirmation of existence" attack. If an attacker can check whether a specific hash exists in the Block Index, they can confirm whether a target user has a particular file (e.g., a known sensitive document). Mitigations: (1) Hash check requires auth: POST /check-blocks requires a valid user OAuth token; the server only returns missing hashes that the caller has upload rights to.
